label: Strait of Hormuz
description: Disruption to commercial transit through the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint for roughly a fifth of seaborne crude. The mechanisms this scenario routes through are the crude price, crude freight rates, marine war-risk premiums and refining crack spreads.
method: Illustrative. Every number in this file was authored by hand to exercise the scenario architecture end to end. None of it is calibrated against history, derived from a model, or elicited from a forecaster, and none of it is a MONAD forecast. It is here so that the strip, the drawer and the bay modules have a shaped, self-consistent scenario to render while the modelling work that would replace it is done.
provenance: hand-authored fixture, docs/research/SCREENER_IA_DRAFT_PLAN.md scenario layer Phase B
partition: The deepest shortfall in daily commercial transits through the strait, measured against the trailing-year baseline and sustained for at least 7 consecutive days, at any point within the horizon. The four branches are half-open intervals on that one quantity — [0,5), [5,20), [20,50), [50,100] percent — so every value falls in exactly one, and their union is the whole range. Endpoints are stated as digits and not in words on purpose, twice over: 'no material shortfall' and 'a limited shortfall of under a fifth' both describe a 1% reading, so a tree built from overlapping English sums to 1 while double-counting; and the 5 and the 7 here are checked against the target's threshold_pct and min_days, which a spelled-out 'seven' would defeat. 'Material' for this scenario means a shortfall of at least 5% on this definition — and that is now enforced rather than promised.

transmission.mechanism: Vessels avoiding or queueing at the strait sail longer routes, so ton-miles rise while the usable fleet shrinks. Freight rates clear higher on the same cargo.
transmission.method: Illustrative transmission edge. The mechanism is a standard one; its strength and confidence are hand-set and not estimated.

transmission.mechanism: Underwriters widen the war-risk area and reprice hull cover, which raises the cost of every transit and is passed into rates on the routes that continue.
transmission.method: Illustrative transmission edge; see the freight-rate edge. Engaged only by the deeper bands because a limited shortfall has historically not moved underwriting.

transmission.mechanism: Barrels that cannot transit are barrels off the market. Non-Gulf supply reprices upward against a shortfall it can only partly replace.
transmission.method: Illustrative transmission edge; strength and confidence are hand-set.

transmission.mechanism: Crude is a refiner's input, and it reprices before products do. The same shortfall that lifts the barrel raises the cost of every barrel run — which is why this edge and the crack edge reach the same bucket with the same sign and land on opposite sides of a refiner's P&L.
transmission.method: Illustrative transmission edge. Present because a scenario that could only express benefit would be the wrong shape: the edge sign is positive (crude rises) and the refiners' sensitivity to that channel is negative, so the derived exposure comes out negative.

transmission.mechanism: A sustained crude shortfall tightens product supply faster than demand falls, widening cracks — but only where the disruption outlasts refiners' inventory cover, which is why the shallow band does not engage this edge.
transmission.method: Illustrative transmission edge, and the lowest-confidence one here: the sign is genuinely contested over short horizons.

developments.summary: Routine multinational minesweeping exercise concludes without incident.
developments.method: Illustrative development. Carries no probability contribution: attributing a number of percentage points to a single event is a modelling claim, and no model here makes it.
